content: If glucose testing is unavailable and hypoglycemia is suspected, initiate empirical treatment and monitor the patient’s response. If glucose levels are confirmed to be low, administer 5 mL/kg of D10 (or 1 mL/kg of D50) for children. For adolescents or adults, provide 125–250 mL of D10 rapidly (or 25–50 mL of D50). Ensure that all maintenance fluids include D5. Additionally, confirm that the child is feeding adequately. For further guidance, refer to the IMAI DCM Quick Check on page 42 or the Child Pocketbook on page 16. For patients experiencing anxiety, provide psychological support as outlined in section 6. In cases of confusion in cooperative patients, calmly and non-aggressively reason with the patient. Keep the lights on at night to reduce disorientation. Administer 5 mg of intramuscular medication (adjusted for the patient’s size) if necessary. Approach the patient cautiously, call for assistance if needed, and only administer treatment if it is safe to do so. Additional details can be found in the IMAI DCM Quick Check on page 60. For unexplained neurological symptoms, consider thiamine deficiency (beriberi) and administer vitamin B1 at a dose of 50 mg intramuscularly or intravenously daily for several days. In managing mild to moderate cases of Ebola, recognize that clinical presentations can vary. Early in the disease course, patients may exhibit mild symptoms such as fever, headache, or fatigue. These patients may still be ambulatory, not experiencing vomiting or significant diarrhea, and able to eat and drink. All patients should be provided with oral rehydration solution (ORS) and encouraged to drink it. Monitor patients every shift to detect progression to severe illness. If the patient remains stable, no further laboratory testing is required after the initial malaria rapid diagnostic test (RDT). For fluid resuscitation, both oral and intravenous fluids should be optimized. Actively encourage patients to take frequent sips of ORS. In confirmed wards, mildly ill patients can assist in supporting ORS intake for more severely ill patients. If nausea or vomiting is present, consider administering an antiemetic such as ondansetron. Offer flavored ORS, coconut water, or mix ORS with fruit juice to improve palatability. Use containers that are easy for the patient to handle while lying in bed, such as a straw or a sippy mug. Ensure the container is accessible by providing a bedside shelf or an appropriately positioned wedge pillow to help weak patients sit semi-reclined for drinking. For children, especially those under two years of age, consider using a nasogastric (NG) tube if fluid intake is insufficient. Liquid feeds (e.g., F-75) can also be administered via the NG tube. Before feeding, confirm the NG tube placement by aspirating or flushing with 10 mL of normal saline without causing the child to cough. To assess whether a patient can rely on ORS for hydration rather than IV fluids, evaluate the adequacy of their ORS intake. Maintain a low threshold for initiating IV hydration if necessary. Check if the patient is too weak to lift the container, monitor how much fluid remains in the container since the last assessment, and observe whether the patient can get out of bed, is vomiting, or has diarrhea (especially large volume or frequent episodes). Assess for signs of shock or dehydration. For moderately unwell children without a caregiver, consider IV fluids. If the patient is stable and shows no signs of severe dehydration or shock, continue offering ORS. If the patient exhibits vomiting, large-volume diarrhea, extreme weakness, poor oral intake, or unconsciousness, IV fluids may be required. For maintenance fluids, calculate the rate based on body weight: 4 mL/kg/hour for the first 10 kg, 2 mL/kg/hour for the next 10 kg, and 1 mL/kg/hour for each additional kilogram. Use adult IV giving sets (20 drops = 1 mL) unless pediatric burettes (60 drops = 1 mL) are required. Employ an electronic infusion pump for accurate titration, especially in children. Monitor for signs of overhydration, such as respiratory distress (pulmonary edema) or peripheral edema (swollen feet). Swollen feet alone should not prompt discontinuation of fluids but should lead to careful reassessment for potential pulmonary edema. When administering IV fluids, healthcare staff must adhere strictly to infection prevention and control (IPC) measures to avoid needlestick injuries and pathogen exposure. Ensure staff are trained and experienced in IV catheter insertion. Gather all necessary equipment, including sharps containers, adhesive dressings, IV catheters, disinfectant swabs, and tourniquets. Use single-use IV catheter preparation kits and safety catheters with shielded retractable needles when possible. Consider one-way valve systems to prevent blood backflow into IV tubing. For patients with difficult IV access, consider early intraosseous access using a powered device if available. Monitor IV sites closely for bleeding and use compression devices if necessary. For Lassa fever and Crimean-Congo hemorrhagic fever (CCHF), ribavirin may be used as treatment or post-exposure prophylaxis for high-risk contacts. Ribavirin is not effective for Ebola or Marburg disease. Its efficacy in Lassa fever and CCHF has not been proven through randomized controlled trials, but observational data suggest it is most effective when administered within the first six days of illness. Ribavirin dosing is 5 mg/kg (maximum 500 mg) every 8 hours for six days, infused slowly in 9% saline. Adjust the dose for patients with renal insufficiency. Monitor for adverse effects, including dose-dependent hemolytic anemia, which typically resolves after treatment cessation. Rapid infusion may cause rigors. Ribavirin is contraindicated in severe anemia, hemoglobinopathies, coronary artery disease, renal insufficiency, decompensated liver disease, breastfeeding, and hypersensitivity. It is teratogenic and contraindicated in pregnancy unless used as a life-saving measure due to high maternal and fetal mortality in Lassa fever. Patients should avoid unprotected sex for six months after ribavirin exposure. For pregnant women with suspected or confirmed Ebola, assess the risk of transmission and document pregnancy status in clinical records. Pregnant women with active Ebola or those who survive without pregnancy loss may transmit the virus during delivery or obstetric care. Ebola in pregnancy is associated with high rates of obstetric complications and poor maternal and perinatal outcomes, including spontaneous abortion, preterm labor, hemorrhage, stillbirth, and neonatal death. Rare cases of recovery without pregnancy loss have been reported. Manage pregnant women in a separate area with privacy and facilities for childbirth and obstetric complications. Provide appropriate fluids, antibiotics, and antimalarial treatment as needed.
